summary: A framework describing the characteristics and use cases for controlling and managing microwave and millimeter wave radio link interfaces using YANG data models. The aim is to unify management of these radio links so they fit into automated, multi-layer network provisioning and operation.

plainLanguage.summary: Radio links that carry internet between towers are all managed in different ways. This sets out why and how to manage them with one common language.

questions: yang for microwave radio link management
how to manage radio link interfaces
subtitle: Framework for unified management of microwave radio links with YANG

tldr.problem: Microwave radio links that carry mobile backhaul between towers are managed differently by each vendor, making multi-vendor networks difficult to automate and operate consistently.
tldr.mechanism: This framework defines what a YANG data model for microwave interfaces should support: configuring radio parameters like frequency and modulation, managing carriers (groups of radio links), monitoring performance and faults, and integrating radio interfaces with the standard Ethernet interface models.
tldr.outcome: A unified YANG data model enables network operators to manage microwave links from multiple vendors through a single controller using standard protocols like NETCONF, improving network automation and reducing operational complexity.

today: RFC 8432 is an Informational RFC providing requirements and framework for YANG models. The IETF CCAMP working group has developed actual YANG models for microwave radio links based on this framework, enabling practical multi-vendor management through standardized protocols.

sections.title: Microwave Technology and Management Challenges
sections.content:
Microwave radio is high-frequency wireless technology used for point-to-point links, primarily as backhaul connecting mobile cell towers. Microwave links operate in frequency bands from 1.4 GHz to above 100 GHz, supporting 1-3 Gbps in traditional bands and up to 10 Gbps in the 70/80 GHz band, with newer systems capable of over 100 Gbps. Microwave is widely deployed because small wavelengths allow narrow directional antennas and high frequencies allow broad bandwidth.

Today, each microwave equipment vendor provides their own management interfaces and parameters. This makes multi-vendor network automation very difficult. Network operators want a standardized YANG data model so that a single Network Management System (NMS) or Software-Defined Networking (SDN) controller can manage microwave interfaces from different vendors alongside standard Ethernet and IP management models, all using NETCONF or RESTCONF protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Microwave radio sends data through the air on radio beams between towers. Each vendor's equipment works differently, so it's hard to automate networks with multiple brands. A standard model would let one controller manage them all.

sections.title: Radio Link Structure and Concepts
sections.content:
A Radio Link Terminal (RLT) is the interface providing Ethernet and Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) capacity on one end of a microwave link. A Carrier Termination is an interface representing the capacity provided over the air by a single carrier (radio channel). A microwave node typically has one RLT connected to several Carrier Terminations, which may be bonded together (aggregated for more capacity) or protected (with 1+1 redundancy).

Carriers can be combined in several ways: aggregation (bonding) increases total capacity, protection provides redundancy so if one carrier fails the other takes over, and nested configurations allow complex arrangements. Understanding this structure is essential for a YANG model to expose the full capabilities of modern microwave equipment while remaining manageable.
sections.plainLanguage: A radio terminal is where the signals enter and leave. One or more radio channels (carriers) work together, either sharing the load or backing each other up. The model needs to describe all these ways to combine them.

sections.title: Management Use Cases and Requirements
sections.content:
The framework identifies six major use cases. Configuration management includes understanding device capabilities, initial setup such as frequency and modulation, and ongoing optimization. Inventory involves retrieving information about radio interfaces and equipment. Status and statistics report real-time performance including effective bandwidth.

Performance management requires configuring and collecting historical measurements. Fault management involves configuring alarms and receiving notifications for radio-specific faults. Troubleshooting requires detailed information to diagnose root causes. All these must be supported in a unified YANG model integrated with existing generic models for devices, interfaces, hardware, and IP management.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators need to set up radio links, see what equipment exists, monitor performance, find out when things break, and figure out why problems happened. All these tasks should work the same way across different vendors.

sections.title: Framework Design Recommendations
sections.content:
The framework recommends building the radio model by extending RFC 8343 (base interface model) with radio-specific parameters, just as other technology models do for Ethernet or IP. This ensures consistency and interoperability with existing management infrastructure. The model should be based on established industry standards like ETSI EN 302 217 (microwave equipment specifications) and should reference existing models from ONF and CCAMP working group efforts.

For generic functionality beyond radio specifics, the model should reference existing RFCs: RFC 8348 for hardware inventory, RFC 8344 for IP management, and a generic YANG alarm model for notifications. The layering of radio, Ethernet, and TDM interfaces should follow the principles in RFC 8343. This modular approach allows the radio-specific parts to be focused while reusing standardized solutions for common functions.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of building everything from scratch, the model should add radio features to the standard interface model used for Ethernet. This keeps everything consistent and lets programs control all link types the same way.

sections.title: Implementation Framework and Scope
sections.content:
The resulting YANG data model (referenced as [IETF-MW]) should support configuration of frequency, channel bandwidth, modulation, coding, and transmitter power for each carrier; aggregation/bonding and protection configurations for radio link terminals; carrier activation/deactivation for optimization; and both read and write operations. It must model the interface layering showing how a Radio Link Terminal provides capacity that feeds into Ethernet or TDM interfaces.

The framework emphasizes leaving room for vendor-specific extensions and product features that go beyond the standardized model. A standard that permits some freedom encourages innovation and competition while ensuring the core management functions work consistently. The goal is unified, multi-vendor automation, not forcing every vendor to implement identically.
sections.plainLanguage: The model will describe all the important controls and settings, but vendors can still add their own special features. This gets everyone talking the same language about the basics while allowing innovation.
